Chapter One: Arriving in a Country on the Edge
Imagine stepping off the plane in Rwanda, right into thick, humid air that clings to your skin. The country’s so green and alive, but there’s something in the atmosphere—a tension that sits just beneath everything, like everyone’s holding their breath, waiting for the next moment to unfold.
The mission? On paper, it’s simple. Keep the peace in a place that’s already seen more violence than anyone should. But reality? It’s never that straightforward.
Those first days go by in a blur. There’s a whirlwind of briefings, quick handshakes, introductions that barely have time to settle in your memory. You watch soldiers, diplomats, aid workers—each one moving through their routines with this careful, measured caution. It’s like everyone’s sizing each other up, quietly wondering, “Who can I really trust here?”
The local leaders—some dressed sharp in crisp uniforms, others in suits that have seen better days—talk about peace, but when you meet their eyes, you see how wary they really are.
In Kigali, the capital, life goes on, sort of. The streets are busy, but not lively. Kids laugh and play in the dust, their voices floating above the hum of old cars. Shopkeepers still arrange their goods with care, but there’s a hush to their conversations, as if they’re watching what they say. The city feels like it’s holding its breath, waiting for something nobody wants to name.
At mission headquarters—a modest building buzzing with radios and covered in maps—the team comes together. It’s a mix of nationalities, backgrounds, and experiences. Some are grizzled peacekeepers who’ve seen it all. Others are new, full of hope, wanting to make a difference, but unsure about what they’ve just walked into.
Those early meetings with Rwandan officials are eye-opening. You start to see just how deep the country’s divisions run. The government, led by one group, keeps insisting everything’s under control. But opposition leaders? They talk quietly, almost in whispers, and their version is much darker. They mention threats, people vanishing, a growing fear that sits heavy in the air.
Pretty soon, it’s clear—the mission’s hands are tied. The rules are strict: observe, report, but don’t get involved unless there’s no other option. Resources are scarce. Not enough vehicles, barely enough radios, and the team is just big enough to cover the capital, but nowhere near enough for the whole country. It’s a recipe for frustration, and you feel it growing every single day.
One afternoon, a local interpreter opens up. He tells you about his family—how neighbors who once shared meals now barely speak, and how everyone keeps glancing over their shoulders in fear of being overheard. It’s a small, quiet moment, but it drives home just how personal these divisions are. They don’t just run through politics—they cut through families, friendships, everyday life.
As days turn into weeks, the warning signs start piling up. You hear about weapons being hidden, militias training out in the hills. Rumors swirl—lists of names, secret plans whispered in the dark. That so-called peace everyone mentions? It’s starting to feel like it could shatter at any moment.
Every evening, the team comes together to debrief. The air’s thick with tension and worry. Some folks argue that more needs to be done, that the mission should push harder to prevent violence. Others warn that stepping in too far could actually make things worse. The responsibility weighs on everyone, and the fear of making the wrong call is always there.
It becomes painfully clear—the mission is stuck somewhere between hope and reality. There’s a real desire to help, but the tools just aren’t there. The world is watching, but from a distance. And for those on the ground, the sense of isolation keeps growing.
You find yourself wondering: what’s it going to take for the world to step in before it’s too late?
